title: AMD Versal RF Series at Hot Chips 2026
gist: AMD's Versal RF Series adaptive SoC pushes wideband RF signal processing (up to 32 GSPS ADC, 18 GHz bandwidth, ~19x DSP compute vs. prior generation) for defense, quantum control, and satellite communications, using hard IP blocks to cut power by up to 87% versus soft FPGA implementations and adding UCIe chiplet expansion for custom RF/AI silicon integration.

insights.claim: AMD claims Versal RF Series delivers up to 19x the DSP compute and 6.4x the maximum sample rate versus its previous generation, reaching 32 GSPS on the ADC side and 18 GHz of RF bandwidth compared with 5 GSPS and 6 GHz on Gen 3, topping out near 80 TOPS of effective DSP compute.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A ~19x compute jump signals AMD is making a major bet on wideband RF/defense/quantum-control markets as a differentiated adjacent business to its core CPU/GPU/FPGA data center lines.
insights.locator: Compute and RF Performance vs. Previous Generation

insights.claim: AMD's integrated RF product timeline runs from the Gen 1 RFSoC parts in 2018 through the 2023 DFE family with RF bandwidth climbing from 4 GHz to 7 GHz, before the Versal RF Series represents what the author calls a 'huge Zynq to Versal 2025 jump.'
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Establishes a multi-generation product cadence in RF silicon that long-cycle defense/aerospace customers rely on for multi-decade system design commitments.

themes.theme: Hard IP as the core efficiency lever

insights.claim: AMD's signal chain runs from the RF-ADC through a first-stage channelizer into the AI Engine array, then a second-stage channelizer and general compute, collapsing an 18 GHz input down toward 1 MHz for analysis — solving the 'drinking from the RF firehose' problem of processing enormous wideband data streams at the edge under size/weight/power limits.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This staged channelization architecture is the core mechanism enabling edge deployment of wideband RF processing without massive off-chip data movement — a template applicable to any wideband sensor-to-AI pipeline.
insights.locator: Problem Statement – Drinking from the RF Firehose

insights.claim: AMD's hard FFT/iFFT blocks sustain 4 GSPS in streaming mode, with VR16xx carrying 28 blocks and VR19xx 36 blocks spanning point sizes 8 to 4096; AMD estimates a hard block uses about 87% lower power than the equivalent soft programmable-logic implementation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: An 87% power reduction from hardening common DSP functions is a striking efficiency number that validates AMD's broader strategy of moving compute from soft FPGA fabric into fixed hard IP blocks for power-constrained deployments.

insights.claim: For a 32K-point FFT at 8 GSPS, running the math on AI Engines plus programmable logic cuts LUT use from over 153,000 down to about 8,000, drops latency from 48 microseconds to 7.5 microseconds, and uses up to 30% lower dynamic power versus a programmable-logic-only structure.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A concrete before/after benchmark (19x fewer LUTs, 6.4x lower latency) demonstrates the tangible payoff of AMD's AI Engine array for wideband DSP, a reusable proof point for justifying adaptive SoC adoption over pure FPGA or ASIC designs.
insights.locator: AI Engines Provide More Compute with Less Power (Example)

insights.claim: AMD frames its device architecture around four compute types trading efficiency for flexibility: hard IP/DSP engines for highest sample rates and common functions, the AI Engine array for wideband processing, and fabric for stitching custom architectures — explicitly putting hard IP where efficiency matters and fabric where flexibility does.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This heterogeneous-compute-tiering framework is a reusable mental model for evaluating any adaptive SoC or accelerator architecture that mixes fixed-function silicon with reconfigurable logic.
insights.locator: Heterogeneous Compute Types Balance Flexibility and Efficiency

insights.claim: Versal RF Series ships as four near-term devices (VR1602, VR1652, VR1902, VR1952) plus a UCIe-capable part; VR1602 uses 16 eight-GSPS ADCs while VR1652 switches to four 32-GSPS ADCs for the highest single-die sampling rate, with VR1902/VR1952 adding more DSP engines and a poly block, all using 14-bit converters.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A four-SKU lineup segmented by sampling rate vs. flexibility gives AMD price/performance tiers to address different defense and test-equipment budget levels.

insights.claim: AMD claims a single VR1602 or VR1652 delivers the equivalent DSP compute of four Virtex UltraScale+ VU13P FPGAs plus the programmable logic/AI Engine resources of a Versal AI Core VC1702, all within a 37.5 x 37.5 mm package.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 4:1 chip consolidation ratio in a small package is a concrete SWaP argument for replacing multi-FPGA RF payloads with a single Versal RF part in size/weight/power-constrained platforms like aircraft or satellites.
insights.locator: AMD Versal RF Size, Weight & Power (SWaP) Advantage

insights.claim: AMD's LDPC decoder hard IP sustains 7.7 Gb/s at eight iterations for 5G NR, 4 Gb/s for DVB-S2, and 3.7 Gb/s for DVB-S2X, with 5G NR support requiring no programmable logic resources; AMD frames four of these decoders as equivalent to a full Virtex UltraScale+ VU13P FPGA.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Targets satellite communications (DVB-S2/S2X) and 5G infrastructure directly, showing AMD's RF silicon addresses commercial telecom/satcom markets alongside defense.

insights.claim: AMD positions Versal RF Series for quantum control applications, sitting between the host GPU/CPU compute stack and the QPU, mapping a latency hierarchy from millisecond-scale error decoding/correction down to nanosecond-scale pulse generation and readout.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Positions AMD as critical classical-control infrastructure for the quantum computing supply chain — an underappreciated adjacent revenue opportunity as quantum computing scales, independent of who wins the QPU race.
insights.locator: AMD Versal RF Series in Quantum Control Applications

insights.claim: The Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK), developed with Fermilab, Oak Ridge National Lab, and the Department of Energy, builds on AMD's RFSoC platform for open qubit control and readout, with Versal RF extending it via higher bandwidth for more read-channel multiplexing and PCIe Gen5/high-speed Ethernet offload.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Direct national-lab and DOE engagement signals AMD's RF silicon has an entrenched position in U.S. government-funded quantum research infrastructure, a durable and less commoditized customer relationship.

insights.claim: Versal RF's UCIe chiplet support exposes UCIe-SP x16 interfaces at up to 16 GT/s and UCIe-AP x64/x32 links, letting designers attach up to four chiplets over a silicon interposer for commercial or custom RF front-end, AI, or specialized compute chiplets.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: UCIe support opens a modular chiplet ecosystem path for custom defense/RF integrators to mix AMD's RF silicon with third-party chiplets — reinforcing UCIe's importance as an interoperability standard across the industry.
insights.locator: AMD Versal RF Series UCIe Chiplet Enablement

themes.theme: Author's read on AMD's post-Xilinx execution

insights.claim: The author sees Versal RF Series as concrete proof that AMD is delivering on the vision Xilinx originally set out for the Versal family years ago, now manifesting as a range of hardened IP paired with flexible FPGA fabric.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Suggests the AMD-Xilinx integration is paying off with tangible product execution years after acquisition, relevant to assessing whether the Xilinx deal has delivered on its strategic rationale.
insights.quote: To me, this is neat because it feels like a concrete example of what I remember Victor describing as Xilinx’s vision when Xilinx launched the Versal family many years ago.
